amendments.rule: **A waw the ASV renders by *also* takes it, wherever in the clause the ASV puts it.** This is rule 14's list — *but*, *then*, *or*, *now* — with the one member that keeps tempting an `added`. English writes *also* postpositively, after the fronted subject or between subject and verb — *Thy gates* ***also*** *shall be open*, *Thou shalt* ***also*** *suck the milk of the nations*, *I will* ***also*** *make thy officers peace* — so the word does not stand where the waw stands, and the unit is discontinuous under rule 25 rather than broken. Distance from the waw is not evidence against it, exactly as in rule 35. The corpus aligns a waw to *also* in 33 units across 21 chapters, so where a waw is present this is settled and the note need not hedge it. **But read whether a waw is present at all before placing the word.** Where no waw stands in the clause, no morpheme licenses the *also* and it is its own `added` unit under rule 30: `אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַשְׁאִיר לְךָ` → *that also shall not leave thee* has only the relative, the negative and the verb, and the *also* answers to none of them. Do not fold such an *also* into the relative, the negative or the verb to avoid the `added`, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* — the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them.
amendments.why: Rule 51's closing sentence asserted that the Old Testament corpus marks no *also* `added` anywhere, and offered that as the evidence settling the rule. DEU.28.51 falsifies it: the ASV writes *that also shall not leave thee* for `אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַשְׁאִיר לְךָ`, where the clause holds no waw at all. Left standing, the sentence tells the next pass that an `added` *also* cannot be right, which would drive it either to hunt for a waw that is not there or to fold the word into a neighbouring unit — the two errors rule 42 already names for the parallel case with *and*. The amendment keeps the whole of the original ruling and its corpus count for the waw-present case, which this chapter does not disturb, and adds the reading for the waw-absent case with the verse that produced it.

amendments.rule: A pronominal suffix aligns to the English pronoun that realizes it, which is usually a possessive or object pronoun: `מִינֵהוּ` → *his kind* splits into the noun and *his*. **The suffix on an infinitive construct is that infinitive's subject and takes the English subject pronoun the ASV writes for it**, while the infinitive keeps the verb: `עַד כַּלֹּתוֹ אֹתְךָ` → *until he have consumed thee* gives *he* to the suffix and *have consumed* to the infinitive, and the object marker and its own suffix are read separately by rules 16 and 11. The ASV's pronoun need not agree in number with the suffix — `עַד הַאֲבִידוֹ אֹתָךְ` → *until they have caused thee to perish* — because the English subject answers to the referent the translation has in view; align the pronoun that is written. This governs only a suffix that is actually present: where none is, a subject pronoun the ASV supplies for an infinitive belongs to the infinitive itself under rules 48 and 52, and rules 40 and 43 dispose of the other places where the English pronoun realizing a morpheme is neither possessive nor object.
amendments.why: Rule 18's *possessive or object* left the commonest remaining case unstated. Rule 40 widens the range only for a preposition the ASV's recasting has silenced, and rules 48 and 52 speak of a subject pronoun the ASV *supplies* where no morpheme carries it — neither covers a suffix that is present and is the infinitive's own subject. DEU.28 met it three times (28.21 `כַּלֹּתוֹ` → *he*, 28.48 `הִשְׁמִידוֹ` → *he*, 28.51 `הַאֲבִידוֹ` → *they*), and the corpus already aligns suffixes of `הוּא` to *he* in 96 units and to *they* in 25, so the amendment records settled practice rather than inventing it. The number clause is included because 28.51 renders a 3ms suffix by *they* and a pass reading only the morphology would mark it `unrepresented` and leave the pronoun `added`. The closing sentence is added so the new clause is not misread as reaching the supplied-subject cases rules 48 and 52 govern.

amendments.rule: The **substantival article** — `הַ` on a participle or adjective used as a noun — takes the pronoun the ASV supplies to make it substantival, and heads on that pronoun rather than on the relative that follows it. `הָרַע` → *that which was evil* is the article with *that which*, headed on *that*; `הָעֹשֶׂה` → *him that doeth* is the article with *him that*, headed on *him*. The supplied pronoun is the article's own rendering and is never `added`. The predicate word keeps its own English, including any copula the ASV supplies, which stays with it under rule 20: in *that which is right*, *is* and *right* belong to the adjective and only *that which* belongs to the article. **An attributive article the ASV renders by a relative goes the same way.** Where `הַ` stands on a participle or adjective modifying an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative instead of a *the* — `אֹיְבֶיךָ הַקָּמִים עָלֶיךָ` → *thine enemies that rise up against thee*, `הָאִישׁ הָרַךְ` → *The man that is tender*, `הַכְּתוּבִים` → *that are written* — the article takes that relative and heads on it, while the participle or adjective keeps its own English together with any supplied copula, exactly as above. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, and where the ASV writes neither the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47.
amendments.why: Rule 41 defined itself as the substantival use and then handed the ordinary attributive article to rule 15's plain *the*, leaving no rule for the case where the article sits on an attributive participle or adjective and the ASV renders it by a relative. Rule 36 already directs a vocative of that shape back to rule 41, so the contract was citing this rule for something its own text excluded. DEU.28 met the case four times and read it one way throughout (28.7 `הַקָּמִים` → *that*, 28.54 `הָרַךְ` → *that* with *is tender* on the adjective, 28.57 `הַיֹּצֵת` → *that*, 28.58 `הַכְּתוּבִים` → *that* with *are written* on the participle), and the corpus aligns `הַ` to *that* in 51 units, among them 1KI.10.8 `עֲבָדֶיךָ אֵלֶּה הָעֹמְדִים` → *these thy servants, that stand*, which is the attributive case and not the substantival one. The final two sentences are added because deciding by what the ASV writes is what keeps rule 15, this rule and rule 29 apart, and because 28.54's second coordinated article shows the sharing case.

conventions: Fused multi-morpheme expressions in this chapter, each one unit under rule 30: ka-asher -> 'as' headed on the preposition (28.9, 28.29, 28.49, 28.63); tachat asher -> 'Because' / 'whereas' (28.47, 28.62); asher ... shammah -> 'whither' across intervening material (28.21, 28.37, 28.63); mi yitten -> 'Would it were' (28.67 twice); kol ha-yamim -> 'alway' (28.29, 28.33); ba-setter -> 'secretly' (28.57); le-maalah / le-mattah -> 'above' / 'beneath' (28.13); mippeney -> 'because of' (28.20) and 'of' (28.60); minneged -> 'before' (28.66); lifney -> 'before' (28.7 twice, 28.25 twice). The counter-case is the one to carry forward: milfaneykha at 28.31 is split three ways, because the ASV writes 'from before thy face' and so spends 'face' on paneh, and kol ha-yom at 28.32 is split three ways for the same reason, because the ASV writes 'all the day'. Read the subtraction test on each occurrence rather than the lemma.

The 'again' of the hiphil of shuv is what that stem contributes and joins the verb's unit, discontinuous under rule 25, rather than being added: heshiv -> 'will bring ... again' at 28.60 and 28.68. Do not read it as a supplied English adverb.

This chapter writes three English 'have's and they go three different ways. 28.40 has hayah present, so hayah takes the 'have' and its le is unrepresented (rule 43, first branch). 28.31 is verbless, so the possessive le takes the 'have' and its suffix takes the subject 'thou' (rule 43, second branch). 28.66's 'shalt have assurance' is a light verb plus complement rendering the hiphil of aman, headed on 'assurance' (rule 44), and is not possessive at all. Test each 'have' by subtraction before reaching for rule 43.

report: Read all 68 verses end to end against the candidate table, the validation report and the corpus rows. No cross-verse split found, so patches is empty.

Every multi-treatment bucket in the candidate table resolves to a difference the ASV licenses rather than to one construction analysed twice. Ha alternates the / this / that / unrepresented according to what the ASV actually writes (28.1 'this day', 28.29 'the blind', 28.54 'that is tender', 28.22's six silent assimilated articles beside the one rendered before 'sword'); be, le, al and min follow the ASV's preposition; natan, shama and hayah follow the ASV's verb phrase.

The ayin clauses are uniform across 28.26, 28.29, 28.31, 28.32 and 28.68: headed on the negation every time. 28.31 diverges only because a possessive le is present there, which is rule 43 rather than a second analysis of ayin.

The two branches of rule 43 are separated cleanly chapter-wide: 28.40 puts 'have' on hayah with its le unrepresented, 28.31 puts 'have' on le because the clause is verbless, and 28.66's 'shalt have assurance' is rule 44's light verb rather than either. Checked deliberately, since a single misreading here would have surfaced as a split.
The presentative frame's 'that' goes to the apodosis waw at 28.1 and 28.15 and stays on the verb at 28.63, where the apodosis opens with ken. That is rule 45's three-way read applied correctly.

The supplied object pronouns marked added (28.13, 28.26, 28.29, 28.31, 28.39, 28.68) agree with each other and with the contrasting cases where an object morpheme is present and takes the pronoun (28.21, 28.51, 28.63). 28.30's 'use the fruit thereof' is not one of these: the suffix is rendered 'thereof' and 'the fruit' belongs to the piel's lexical rendering, headed on 'use'.

Fusion is uniform, and the one place the chapter refuses to fuse is refused for the right reason: milfaneykha at 28.31 splits three ways because the ASV spends 'face' on paneh, while lifney at 28.7 and 28.25 fuses to 'before'. Same test at 28.20 and 28.60 for mippeney.

The object marker takes English exactly once, at 28.29 ('prosper in thy ways'), and is unrepresented in all 32 other occurrences. Subtraction confirms it: drop the 'in' and only the object relation is diminished, since derekh keeps 'ways'. Corpus has three aligned et to 'in'.

BSB: no genuine error. The four counted classes (Td 24, R 29, Sd 6, To 9) are the documented convention difference. Both singletons verify correct. 28.35's waw stands between the two limits of 'from the sole ... unto the crown', where the ASV writes no 'and'. 28.48's ennu is a resumptive object suffix that the ASV's plain relative spends no word on, handled as 28.60's hem is, and distinct from 28.49's 'whose' and 28.52's 'wherein' where the English word does carry the pronoun's sense.

Rule 51's corpus claim is now false. 28.51's 'also' in 'that also shall not leave thee' has no waw anywhere in the clause and is correctly added, which is the first added 'also' in the Old Testament. Amended rule 51 so a later pass does not hunt for a waw or fold the word into a neighbouring unit to avoid the added.

Two further amendments fill gaps this chapter met repeatedly and the corpus already fills in practice: a suffix on an infinitive construct taking the English subject pronoun (28.21, 28.48, 28.51, the last against number with haavido rendered 'they'), and an attributive article rendered by a relative (28.7, 28.54, 28.57, 28.58; 1KI.10.8 does the same and no rule states it).

Two readings examined and left as accepted, both single-verse and both defensible: 28.50 gives 'of' to the construct adjective az rather than to panim, on the ground that the 'of' attaches the whole attributive phrase to 'nation' rather than expressing the chain; and 28.68 folds the supplied subject noun of 'no man' into the ayin unit as rule 21's dummy subject is folded. Neither note names its competitor, which is a soft point under rule 8 but not an edge error, and neither is a cross-verse matter.
Nothing was re-validated because nothing was changed. The 1617 units, the ledger partition and the recorded heads stand as the verse passes returned them.
